title: {{NAME}} and the Unicorn Who Couldn't Gallop
moral: Everyone has a different kind of magic, and yours is exactly right for you.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a shimmering lilac-white shirt, silver-grey shorts, and rainbow-laced sneakers — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
The unicorn appeared in the meadow at the edge of town just after sunrise, and {{NAME}} was the first one to see her.

She was smaller than he expected: about the size of a large pony, with a horn that spiralled silver-gold and a mane the colour of clouds just before rain.

She was also, clearly, limping.

{{NAME}} sat very still at the fence until she looked at him. Then he said quietly: "I won't come any closer unless you want me to."

She walked straight up and pressed her nose to his palm.

pages.content:
Her name was something like a chord of music, three notes his voice couldn't quite make, so he called her Silver.

Silver's problem was her left foreleg. Not injured, he realised on closer inspection. Just differently shaped, turned slightly inward.

She could walk fine. She could canter if she worked at it. But she couldn't gallop, the thundering earth-shaking gallop that all the other unicorns in her herd could do.

The animals of the meadow understood. The rabbits never ran past her at full speed. The deer kept their pace when she walked with them.

pages.content:
"You don't need to gallop," {{NAME}} told her one afternoon. "Watch what you can do instead."

Silver's horn glowed when she was near animals that were ill or frightened. A warm spiral of golden light that moved from the tip of her horn into whatever she touched.

The lame sparrow she touched: flew by morning.

The anxious fox cub who had been too scared to eat: ate the same evening.

The old tortoise with cloudy eyes: blinked, and his gaze cleared.

"See?" said {{NAME}}. "That's not something the other unicorns can do."

pages.content:
Word spread. The meadow animals began coming to Silver deliberately: a badger with a sore ear, a squirrel who'd been out of sorts for a week, a very elderly hedgehog who just liked the warmth.

Silver healed what she could and stayed close for the rest.

{{NAME}} watched her one afternoon working through a queue of animals, unhurried and patient.

She glanced at him. Her horn pulsed once, gently.

"You're the best healer in the whole meadow," he said.

Her ears went up in a way he had come to recognise as happiness.

pages.content:
That evening, as {{NAME}} got ready for bed, he looked out his window at the meadow.

In the twilight, Silver was walking slowly along the fence line, her horn a soft glowing thread in the dusk.

Behind her, following in a quiet line: rabbits, a fox, two deer, a badger, a squirrel, and the elderly hedgehog.

Not keeping up with her. Walking at her pace. Choosing to.

{{NAME}} watched until they disappeared into the dark, then got into bed feeling full of something he didn't have a word for yet.

Outside, very faint, he heard the meadow settle: grass, and quiet animals, and the soft hum of a silver horn.
